naturalness.evidence: “What were the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath commanded to do?” is idiomatic English. Both “going off duty” and “commanded to do” are familiar constructions, and their combination requires no wording repair.

processing.evidence: Readers must retain “What were” across “the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath” until reaching “commanded to do.” They must also distinguish the identifying duty transition from the requested action. This is an ordinary, manageable demand: the modifier identifies the relevant divisions, and the passive does not require recovering the commander.

context_economy.evidence: There is no additional introduction or option text. “The two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath” economically identifies the group being asked about; the question contains no unnecessary setup.

structure_assessments.reason: In “the two divisions going off duty on the Sabbath,” the adjacent modifier naturally attaches to “divisions,” while “on the Sabbath” locates the duty transition. Retaining that group until “commanded” creates only a short, ordinary dependency and serves the intended identification.

“Commanded to do” conventionally presents the divisions as both recipients of the command and performers of the requested action. Although readers must separate “going off duty” from what they were commanded to do, the wording clearly marks those functions without requiring identification of the commander.
